eyebrow: Python for Data Engineers · Chapter 5, Lesson 28
subtitle: execute(), executemany(), and the commit you can't skip.

code:
cursor.execute(
    "INSERT INTO Production.ProductCategory "
    "(Name, rowguid, ModifiedDate) "
    "VALUES (?, NEWID(), GETDATE());",
    ("Test Category",)
)
conn.commit()
conn.close()
caption: The ? placeholder -- the value is passed separately, never pasted into the string.

eyebrow: Many rows at once with executemany()
code:
rows = [
    ("Trail Runner GTX", 2, 129.99),
    ("Alpine 2P Tent", 1, 249.50),
    ("Summit Daypack 22L", 1, 79.00),
]

cursor.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO Staging.ProductSnapshot "
    "(ProductName, Quantity, UnitPrice) VALUES (?, ?, ?);",
    rows
)
conn.commit()
caption: Same statement, once per row -- the driver batches the round trips to the server.

eyebrow: Forget commit(), and it never happened
code:
cursor.execute(
    "INSERT INTO Staging.ProductSnapshot (ProductName) "
    "VALUES (?);",
    ("Untracked Row",)
)
# conn.commit()  <- forget this, and SQL Server rolls
#                   it back when the connection closes
conn.close()
caption: pyodbc connections are NOT in autocommit mode by default.

code:
cursor.execute("TRUNCATE TABLE Staging.ProductSnapshot;")
cursor.executemany(
    "INSERT INTO Staging.ProductSnapshot "
    "(ProductName, Quantity, UnitPrice) VALUES (?, ?, ?);",
    rows
)
conn.commit()
caption: Truncate the staging table first, so it only ever holds the current run's data.

subtitle: Why that ? placeholder isn't just a style choice.
